title: kubelet-oom-and-cni-dns-latency-triage-notes
content:
Summary:

Short: Between 2025-02-11 02:12 UTC and 2025-02-11 04:00 UTC we saw transient 5xx error spikes and elevated p95 API latency for the hosted inference endpoints. Root cause chain appears to be a combination of kubelet OOM/thrashing on a subset of worker nodes and concurrent CNI packet processing delays that caused CoreDNS resolution timeouts and connection stalls. The two failure modes amplified each other: pods restarted due to OOMs and restarted pods generated bursts of control traffic; CNI latency caused kubelet health checks and kube-proxy flows to slow, increasing resource pressure and more OOMs.

What we observed (customer impact):
- ~8% of requests to /v1/generate returned 502/504 during the window; error logs show network connection failures followed by application-level timeouts.
- Increased pod restarts for model-serving replicas (~70 restarts across 6 nodes in 90m).
- CoreDNS latency p95 jumped from ~12ms to ~420ms for the cluster, correlated with the same timeframe.
- Node-level memory reclaim events and OOM kills observed on 6 nodes.

Timeline (quick):
- 02:10 UTC: Synthetic monitors alert: p95 latency > SLA for hosted-api.
- 02:12 UTC: Pager fired to SRE rotation. On-call pulled logs and saw DNS timeouts and backend connection resets.
- 02:20 UTC: Noted repeated kubelet evictions logged in journal: "kubelet eviction manager: "kubelet eviction manager: threshold met" and kernel OOM killer entries for containerd-shim and model process.
- 02:35 UTC: Found netfilter conntrack high usage on nodes (nf_conntrack_count ~ close to nf_conntrack_max) and increased tcp_retransmit/retries counters.
- 02:45 UTC: Cordon+drain started on two worst nodes to stop churn; immediate reduction in pod restarts and some recovery in CoreDNS latency after re-scheduling to healthy nodes.
- 03:20 UTC: Manual bump of sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max + cleared conntrack table on two nodes.
- 03:50 UTC: Alerts cleared; monitoring shows API error rate back to baseline. Post-facto investigation continued (this doc).

Key evidence/log snippets (redacted):
- kernel: Out of memory: Kill process 23567 (containerd-shim) score 987 or sacrifice child
- kubelet: eviction manager: attempting to reclaim ephemeral-storage, memory
- coredns[proxy]: read udp 10.0.0.10:53->10.0.0.34:58731: i/o timeout
- conntrack: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet

Root cause hypothesis (chain):
1) A burst of short-lived control-plane and client connections (likely from recent rollout/scale event + traffic spike) increased active connection counts.
2) Conntrack table max was near default (~262144) on some instance types; simultaneous increase pushed it over the limit -> packet drops and TCP retransmits.
3) CNI dataplane (we run Calico on these clusters) showed increased per-packet latency under load; this compounded the DNS latency symptom because DNS requests to CoreDNS pods were delayed or dropped.
4) Pods experienced delayed readiness and higher CPU/memory transient usage; kubelet eviction thresholds were hit on nodes with marginal memory headroom, triggering OOM kills and restarts. Pod churn caused more ephemeral connections and a feedback loop.

Immediate mitigations executed (what worked):
- Cordon + drain of two highest-pressure nodes, keeping daemonsets up (drain with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data when safe). This stopped churn locally and allowed quick rescheduling.
- Scale-up: temporarily increased node group desired count + autoscaler disabled scale-down for 30m to absorb load.
- Cleared conntrack table on affected nodes: `sudo conntrack -F` and raised `sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288` as a short-term fix.
- Restarted CoreDNS deployment sequentially (rolling restart, 1Pod at a time) to recover healthy DNS responses.
- Increased kube-proxy replicas on some AZs to reduce NAT pressure.

Commands run during triage (useful for runbook):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels
- kubectl top node; kubectl top pod -n hosted-api
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | grep -i evict
- sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count; sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
- sudo conntrack -L | wc -l; sudo conntrack -F
- kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx --since=30m
- ss -s; ss -tn state established | wc -l

Why this is unique / interesting (notes to self):
- Not a pure memory leak or single broken pod: evidence points to an emergent systems-level interaction (conntrack limits + CNI latency + kubelet eviction defaults) that only showed up under this particular traffic profile and node instance type.
- We have historically tuned nf_conntrack for older instance types; newer instance families with higher TCAM/conntrack headroom may not exhibit this. The mix across a heterogeneous fleet is part of the reason only some nodes were affected.

Short-term follow-ups (owners):
- Increase default nf_conntrack_max on node boot images for this fleet (infra: Tom Berger). Ticket JIRA-4581.
- Add an alert when nf_conntrack_count > 80% for >5m (sre: Aisha).
- Add a runbook step: if conntrack table near full -> cordon nodes, clear conntrack, raise conntrack_max temporarily, then monitor. (sre: Miguel).
- Review kubelet eviction thresholds on this node group and set higher soft eviction thresholds for memory/ephemeral-storage to avoid thrash during short bursts (eng-serving-runtime: Renee Zhao).
- Investigate Calico dataplane configs: check iptables vs eBPF mode, MTU mismatches, and per-node BPF map limits. Possible work item to migrate troubled clusters to eBPF dataplane if not already. (netteam: TBD).

Longer-term / architectural changes to consider:
- Proactive conntrack sizing for autoscaled groups and better node image defaults. Document normative nf_conntrack_max by instance family.
- Improve autoscaler reaction to sudden connection-based load (scale-up earlier on connection spikes).
- Instrument connection churn metrics per deployment (established TCP count per pod) and add anomaly detection.
- Consider kubelet config tuning: eviction soft thresholds with longer grace periods for model-serving deployments that have short CPU/memory spikes.
- Add coreDNS horizontal autoscaling by observing request load per pod and latency.

Unresolved questions / investigation items:
- What caused the initial burst of short-lived connections? Recent deploys? CI job? Customer traffic pattern? Need to cross-check with GH-redirector#312 and API gateway logs.
- Which kernel/AMI combinations show this behaviour most often? Do we have an image-level regression?
- Did any other control-plane components (kube-proxy, iptables conntrack) log rate-limits or OOMs? Need deeper node-level telemetry.

Draft runbook excerpt (quick):
Triage: If users see increased 5xx and CoreDNS latency:
1) Check CoreDNS p95 in monitoring and `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide`
2) Check node conntrack counts: `sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count` and `nf_conntrack_max`
3) If conntrack > 80% across >2 nodes: cordon and drain the worst nodes, clear conntrack (`conntrack -F`), and raise `nf_conntrack_max` temporarily on affected nodes.
4) If kubelet evictions present: inspect `journalctl -u kubelet`, identify OOM kills, and consider temporary scale-up and cordoning to stop churn.
5) Restart CoreDNS pods one at a time if DNS errors persist.
6) Post-mitigation: open ticket for infra to bake conntrack tuning into AMI and add alerts.

Notes for postmortem: keep this doc as draft; gather correlation with deployment logs and API gateway. If we confirm rollout triggered the initial spike, include deployment rollback mitigation and gated rollout plans.

Attachments / data to collect for postmortem:
- node-level sysctl snapshots for affected and unaffected nodes for the window
- coredns pod logs and request traces (link to GH-redirector#312 trace)
- kubelet journal excerpts with timestamps
- autoscaler events and API gateway request surge window

Concluding remark:
This incident is an example of how hard-to-observe kernel-level limits (conntrack) + dataplane latency can cascade into application-visible failures through kubelet eviction behavior. The actionable items are clear: surface conntrack early, tune defaults, and make kubelet eviction behavior more forgiving for short-lived bursts for our model-serving workloads.

-- Aisha (on-call)
